title: Dongshan's Hot and Cold
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk is that true freedom and liberation come from embracing our own preferences and desires, rather than trying to escape or control them. By fully experiencing and accepting what arises in life, we can burn up or freeze in a way that allows us to live more authentically and without resistance. This approach requires letting go of judgment and attachment, and instead trusting in the mind's ability to straighten itself out, allowing us to meet each moment with greater ease and awareness.

sentences.text: I had to boot up.
Cliff Record, case 43.
The Pointer.
*Ten thousand ages abide by the phrase that determines heaven and earth.
Even the thousand sages cannot judge the ability to capture tigers and rhinos.
Without any further traces of obstruction, the whole being appears everywhere, equally.
If you want to understand the hammer and tongs of transcendence, you need to forge with the [unclear: "bellow"] of an adept.
But say, since ancient times, has there ever been such a family style or not?
To test, I'm citing this old case.
Look.*
The case.
*A monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat come, how can we avoid them?"
Dongshan said, "Why don't you go to a place where there is no cold or heat?"
The monk said, "Where is the place with no cold or heat?"*
*Dongshan said, "When it's cold, the cold kills you.
When it's hot, the heat kills you."
The monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat come, how can we avoid them?"
Dongshan said, "Why don't you go to a place where there is no cold or heat?"
The monk said, "What is that place where there is no cold or heat?"
Dongshan said, "When it's cold, the cold kills you.
When it's hot, the heat kills you."*
And [unclear: "Suedo"], who collected this koan in his book, wrote a verse.
He wrote:
*He lets down his hand, but it's still the same as the ten thousand fathom cliff.
Why must correct and biased be in an arrangement?
The ancient crystal palace reflects the bright moon.
The sly hound of Han vainly runs up the stairs.
He lets down his hand, but still it's the same as the ten thousand foot cliff.
Why must correct and biased be in an arrangement?
The ancient crystal palace reflects the bright moon.
The ancient crystal palace reflects the bright moon.
And the sly hound of Han runs vainly up the stairs.*
Why then, with a reputation for inscrutability, do we start a talk in such a way?
But we do.
It's a traditional talk.
I'm told that when people ask the Dalai Lama what Buddhism is all about, he just says, "Everybody wants to be happy."
That's what the Dalai Lama, I'm told, says about Buddhism.
And that is true.
That is the case.
Everybody wants to be happy.
And that's true in this koan, this old story.
The monk has noticed that he has some preferences about weather, about the temperature.
Maybe over time, as he's been practicing meditation and living in the Zen monasteries, he's noticed how thoroughly obsessed the mind can be with preferences.
How many things we wish were just a little bit different.
How many things we want, how many things we don't want.
And maybe over time he'd been noticing that even though he'd done all this practice, it just seems to get worse in a way.
You just become more sensitive.

You become more aware of how caught in wishes and desires and preferences the mind is about everything: temperature, food, the way that things are done, your friends, your family, your co-workers, yourself.
Those preferences can really run your life and run your happiness.
When conditions happen for some strange reason to be in a line, more or less, with your preferences, things are pretty good, but then they never last.
Never last.
And then things are not so good.
It's really pretty clear, as we look at our mind, that on the whole, preferences get in the way of being happy, and yet they seem to be deeply wired in, strongly trending forward in the mind.
You might know this talk is part of a project.
My teacher made a list of twenty-five of these old Zen stories, Zen koans, from some of the different koan collections.
I've been slowly working my way through, giving a talk on each of these twenty-five cases, and there's about five left.
It's taken me a couple of years.
I've got a list on the [unclear: "bullet board"] where I check them off.
One day I'll have a little party and throw it away.
Recycle it.
I looked at the list of the ones that weren't checked off, and this one about hot and cold naturally jumped out at me.
My wife told me, did you know this, that yesterday was the hottest recorded day on record in Bellingham in known history?
At least that's what the paper said.
So heat, or heat anyway, is on our mind.
But how could there be any heat if we didn't have some idea of cold?
And even though this case sounds like it, it's not really, of course, about heat and cold anyway.
It's about the mind.
It's about happiness.
It's about suffering.

You might think, when you notice this tendency of the mind to put everything that emerges in two camps, like "I like it," "I don't like it," "it only needs to be this way or not that way," that there would be a way to stop that.
You might think that, that maybe if we practiced long enough or worked with the mind skillfully enough, it would just shut up after a while.

And while it actually is true that one can have experiences, in life and in meditation both, where the mind is quieter, where one is more fully merged with the actual present moment and preferences are not so loud, it turns out it's not possible to rewire the mind and get rid of preferences and just cruise blissfully through life.
If you try to do that, you're just going to create more trouble and a new level of preferences.
So the monk was trying to figure out what to do.
He had this idea that maybe there is a way, if you just practiced hard enough or learned the right teaching.
If he just asked his teacher Dongshan the right question, maybe there would be some special teaching to help him liberate himself from this stickiness with preferences.
So he asked, when cold and heat come, when preferences come, how can we avoid them?
And Dongshan said, why don't you go to a place where there is no cold or heat?
Which is a Zen way of saying there is no such place.
They are kind of tricky that way.
Why don't you just go to where there is no cold and heat?
In other words, no way, you can't do it.
And the monk didn't get it, apparently.
So he asked a follow-up question.
This is typical of these encounters, just to give us something to chew on.
Usually the monk asks a question, the teacher gives a pithy answer, and the monk doesn't quite get it and has to ask a follow-up question.
In a way it cheers us up, because these are serious Zen students.
They must have been much better meditators than us.
And even still, they don't get it.
So the monk asked again, well, where is that?
Okay, where is the place with no cold or heat?
And so Dongshan has to straighten him out, and straighten us out.
When it's cold, the cold kills you.
When it's hot, the heat kills you.
In other words, you can't get out of it.
You can only go through it.
You can only enter into your life as it is, fully.
You can only burn up and freeze to death.
Fully experience your preferences, and fully feel in your body and mind and your heart what that is.
The full play of joy and suffering that emerges from that cycle of desire and aversion.
It's actually true that we do allow ourselves, to a greater or lesser extent, to be run and controlled by our preferences.
But we don't usually know.
We don't usually notice that.
This is where it's good to have two things in your life.
One good thing to have to study the way preferences run your life is other people in your life.
You can't really figure this out on your own.
Another good thing to have is meditation practice.
When you study other people, you can often see their preferences just pushing them around: "I have to have this.
I need that.
I hate that.
I hate it when they do that."
Being in the passenger seat of a car is a good time to study this.
Why is he so upset?
It's just a red light.
A 19-year-old in a fast car.
It's just whatever it is.
But then you don't realize, when you're in the driver's seat, that you too are doing the same thing.
Your own preferences make sense.
They are normal.
They're just how people are.
They're the way people ought to think and behave.
So our own preferences seem perfectly justified and sensible.
And it causes a great amount of trouble that the rest of the universe doesn't seem to get it.
And would they please all cooperate a little better in lining things up with my preferences?
Formal Zen practice is also a good way to study preferences, because we have all these rules and guidelines about what to do.
We simplify the conditions of life down for a little while: for an evening, for a day, for a week.
We just sit down and sit still when the bell rings and stand up when it rings again.
We don't get to decide, like, "Oh, I think this has been enough."
That really helps us study our preferences.
In a little bit longer retreat you can still study.
It's the same pattern throughout the day.
Eating and walking.
There's nothing you really get to decide about.
Nothing that you really could have any preference about.
You just do the thing, right?
You live a very simple life on the formal Zen retreat.
Everything is decided for you.
So you would think that the mind of preferences would settle down.
But actually how it's useful is that your preferences become so ridiculous that you see them a little more clearly.
One can become obsessed about things.
When you're walking along in the slow walking meditation you do, at the corner you have to turn, right?
You can be obsessed with the person in front of you, and it always turns in a really screwy way.
Or whatever it is.
It's sort of silly what it could be.
I often tell a story about when I was three months in the monastery, the sort of more formal monastery in our school.
I got really obsessed and angry about the way you'd eat all the meals in the meditation hall too.
It's a very concentrated experience.
You eat the meals in the meditation hall and everything's ritualized, and you bow and you chant and you bow and you do this and you do that.
One of the things that you do is you pass the condiments in a particular way.
You turn and you hold it in a particular way and they take it in a particular way and you bow together.
And the mind actually generated an enormous amount of judgment and anger about my one neighbor on this side.
He had this really sort of stiff, arrogant way of passing the condiments, and it really bothered me.
It was a big part of my experience with this guy.
I thought he was a real prick.
It was most of my preferences taking hold, my judgments.
It wasn't really anything to do with him or anything to do with me exactly.
It was the mind functioning.
And me having the opportunity, whether I particularly noticed I was having this opportunity or not is questionable, but me having the opportunity to study the mind.
What else is great about these old stories is they're sort of like the family stories.
They're sort of the family jewels of our Dharma family.
Like all family stories, they're a little bit idealized and particular to particular people.
In our particular school, the teachers from about the seventh through the tenth century in China are much talked about.
I'm sure there were a lot of practitioners since the tenth century, but these are who we focus on in our family stories.
So this is a Dongshan.
An important ancestor.
His name in Japanese is Tozan, and the To in Tozan is the same as the To in Soto Zen.
So he's one of the two founding teachers of this particular school, the Soto Zen school.
In China, he lived from 807 to 869, so ninth century China in the Tang dynasty.
As a child, maybe 11 or 12, he famously was going to the Sunday services at the temple.
They would chant the Heart Sutra, like we chant the Heart Sutra here.
One time he famously asked the village priest about the Heart Sutra.
He asked about that part that talks about no eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue, no mouth.
He asked the priest, "I have eyes, I have a nose, I have a tongue, what does this mean?"
The local priest was so impressed by this question that he sent young Dongshan off to the monastery for further training.
He went off very early, ordained very early, and by the time he was 21 he was fully ordained, which I'm not yet myself, so these guys were.
And he studied, anyway, what's with you people though?
How come you never wonder about that line?
Do you think you don't have eyes?
It seems odd.
We're too polite, I guess, to ask about these weird things that we do.
We'll have that Heart Sutra class one time, we'll study that point.
Why does it say that anyway?
Maybe it's a good teaching for us not to be so polite, to actually ask the questions.
Anyway, Dongshan studied with three of the famous teachers of the age, also sort of selectively memorialized later.
This was the Golden Age of Zen, they called it.
He studied with Nanquan, Kuishan, and Yunyan, who are in several other, all of whom are in other koans.
So we can kind of trace the stories of these people through these little stories, these little encounters, through the eighth and ninth and tenth centuries.

The other thing I think that's interesting about Zen history, which is somehow very human, is that these family stories of Zen, these great teaching stories of these koans, were collected and written down in the next era, in the Song Dynasty.
And the Song scholars and teachers are the ones that said the previous time, the Tang Dynasty, was the Golden Age of Zen.
Why is it that the previous one is always better?
The Golden Age always happened a little while ago, the Golden Age can never be now.
And you think about it, we do that all the time.
So I could think to myself, "If only I'd been born a little earlier, at the right time, I could have studied with Suzuki Roshi, oh, that would have been good.
That was the Golden Age, for sure."
It's interesting that we do that, and it's another kind of preference, right?
We actually prefer a completely different time than we have.
Anyway, a little more about doing Zen.
His enlightenment story is very beautiful, too.
After studying for many years, when he was leaving Yunyan's place, Dongshan asked his teacher, "How should I describe the Dharma if someone asks me about it after you have passed away?"
It's always such a beautiful question, a little different cultural attitude, you know.
Next time you see your teacher, do you say, "Well, what if you die?
How will I describe your teaching?
How will I memorialize you?
How should I remember you, teacher?"
It's so beautiful.
And Yunyan answered, "Just that."
Dongshan didn't really understand what that meant.

As he was walking along, and I'm actually convinced that walking from one monastery to another was a big part of their practice, because they didn't have cars or maybe they couldn't afford donkeys, but they did a lot of walking.
You look at maps of China and the places these guys went, and they would often walk 100 miles or more to get to the next place.
So as he was walking along, presumably, he was turning over these last words of Yunyan to him in his mind, studying that phrase, "just that."
Repeating it to himself, "just that."
Breathing, "just that."
As he gazed at trees and villages, as he looked at mountains and rivers, "just that."
And then one time when he was crossing a stream, probably on a hot sunny day, like we've been having, he looked down at the water and he saw his reflection.
Somehow he really saw his reflection, and he had a great experience of enlightenment, of awakening.
He started teaching when he was 50 years old, settling in at a small monastery on the slopes of a mountain called [unclear: "Dung"], Mount [unclear: "Dung"].
He took his name from that: Dongshan.
Shan means mountain, and a lot of them were on mountains.
So: cold and warm, uncomfortable, relaxed, noisy or quiet, this way or that way.
We have so many preferences.
Here's another Zen teaching about this.
It's a very famous poem from about the fifth century, by another Zen teacher in China.
Some centers chant it every day in the service to try to bring this point home about preferences.
This is the Xing Xing Ming.
This author translates that title as "Trust in Mind."
Can you trust the mind?
It's a long poem.
*The great way is not difficult for those who have no preferences.
When love and hate are both absent, everything becomes clear and undisguised.
Make the smallest distinction, however, and heaven and earth are set infinitely apart.
If you wish to see the truth, then hold no opinions for or against anything.
To set up what you like against what you dislike is a disease of the mind.
When the deep meaning of things is not understood, the mind's essential peace is disturbed to no avail.
The way is perfect, space.
There is nothing lacking.
There is nothing in excess.
It is just due to our choosing to accept or reject that we do not see the true nature of things.
Live neither in the entanglement of outer things, nor the inner feeling of emptiness.
Be serene in the oneness of things, and such erroneous views will disappear by themselves.
But when you try to stop activity to achieve passivity, your very effort fills you with activity.*
Just good meditation advice, actually.
You try to stop activity to achieve passivity, and your very effort fills you with activity.
*As long as you remain in one extreme or the other, you will never know oneness.
Those who do not live in the single way fail in both activity and denial.
To deny the reality of things is to miss their reality.
To assert the emptiness of things is to miss their reality.
The more you talk and think about it, the further astray you wander from the truth.
Stop talking and thinking, and there is nothing you will not be able to know.*
Which is classic Zen: somebody writing a poem telling you to stop thinking.
*At the moment of inner enlightenment there is going beyond appearance and emptiness.
The changes that appear to occur in this empty world we call real only because of our ignorance.
Do not search for the truth.
Only cease to cherish opinions.
Do not remain in that dualistic state.
Avoid such pursuits carefully.
If there is even the trace of this and that, of right and wrong, the mind-essence will be lost in confusion.*
[unclear: "We'll make that enough"].
It goes along for some more pages in that vein.
And this makes me think also of what I was saying a couple of weeks ago about the Thai teacher [unclear: "Ki Naniyan"] emphasizing just stability.
Not trying to figure things out or solve our problems, but to see if we can find, through our practice, neutrality: the quiet space in the middle of all these preferences.
A few years ago on Samish Island our guiding teacher Norman Fischer also made some comments on this exact same case, it turns out.
He makes more or less the same points that I'm trying to make, but maybe it's helpful to hear it with other words.
Let me read you a little bit of a [unclear: "Dharamitaki"] on Samish Island.
This is really an important point, and we're so used to our preferences that it's really hard to see them clearly.
*So the monk is asking,* this is Norman, *he's saying, "OK, I see how my preferences are causing suffering.
When it's hot I want it to be cooler.
When it's warm I want it to be cooler.
This is how it goes all the time in my life, and I can't control the weather, so I'm unhappy.
So what am I going to do?
How am I going to go beyond my habit of preference?
And this seems to me to be really difficult, if not impossible.
The closer I look at my mind, the more I see how many preferences I have.
In fact, I'm looking and I'm looking really, really closely, and I see that there's basically nothing there but preferences one after another.
Moment after moment after moment after moment of desire, aversion, desire, aversion, preference, disappointment, over and over again.
There are situations in life when this is obvious, but even when it's not obvious it's going on all the time.
If I fulfill my desire after lots of effort and it works out, for a moment I'm really happy, I'm elated.
But very quickly it all wears out and I'm dissatisfied again.
Or I can't fulfill desire and then I'm complaining, I'm whining, I'm convinced the world is against me, that my life is tragic, and so on.
And either way it's a problem, and this is how it is constantly.
For a long time I went on this way, constantly trying to find the perfect situation, making all these adjustments, not really realizing what a trap it was.
But now I've practiced long enough and I see, I really see, this is a trap.
And I'm desperate.
I'm caught.
I can't see a way out.
What am I going to do?"*
So Norman says, this is what the monk is asking.
And I think we can all relate to this question.
Dongshan's answer to him is, "When it's cold, the cold kills you, and when it's hot, the heat kills you."
What he's telling the monk is Don't try to find a place beyond your preferences.
Don't think you can escape from preference and be a preferenceless ideal abstraction.
Instead, embrace what's in front of you, whatever happens.
Whatever you're feeling or thinking or experiencing, embrace it.
Turn towards it.
Make use of it.
Give yourself to it without reservation, whatever it is.
If you will make use of it, if you will give yourself to it completely, you will allow change and letting go and growth and development to happen.
And then you'll be able to come over to what's next, fresh, and you'll be ready.
That's what Dongshan is telling the monk.
And then Norman tells the story.
He came a day late to the sesshin, you remember this, a few years ago.
He came a day late because he had to go to a party, and he was telling about the party.
Earlier he said something about it, so he goes on about the party.
At the party the other night, my wife Cathy and I were sitting together.
I had on one side an old friend, a dharma teacher, who I know well.
And she had on her side an old friend of our host, an elderly woman who was very lively and chatty.
So I spent the evening talking with my friend about all these different things, having a nice time.
And she was talking to this woman.
And on the way home in the car, I said to her, well, did you enjoy the evening?
Did you enjoy talking to that woman?
Was she interesting?
Or was it more a case of being stuck with someone you didn't really enjoy and having to spend the evening with her?
And so my wife said, both.
And I said, well, what do you mean both?
And she said, if you can't be with the one you love, love the one you're with.
You all recognize that line from the Sixties song.
I thought that was a wise saying of my wife.
This is kind of poignant because now several of us got to spend some time with Norman's wife just the other day.
And actually, it's precisely Dongshan's point.
"Let the cold kill you" means whether you like the cold or you don't like the cold, you can just delightfully disappear into the cold and be liberated by it.
You can like it.
You can know you like it.
You can enjoy that.
You can dislike it.
You can know that you dislike it.
You can complain.
But either way, and beyond both, you can disappear fully into this moment of your life and be liberated by it.
And be free to meet the next moment, fresh, not stuck on the previous.
And why not do that?
What else are you going to do?
What else are you going to do when a moment of your life arrives right where you are, emerging from conditions in the endless past?
What are you going to do when that happens?
Run away?
Try to change it?
Try to make the moment into another moment?
Because here it is, an unrepeatable shining moment.
For a second, and then it's gone.
What choice is there but to meet each moment?
To embrace it and to let yourself be wonderfully finished off by that moment in your life.
I thought that was a nice way of putting it.
So may I close my talk with the last little thing about Dongshan, our relative.
The story that's recorded about his dying days is really beautiful.
The way it's recorded, you can really feel his commitment to practice to the very end, and how much he cared for his students.
*A monk asks, when the master is not well, is there someone who is well or not?
Dongshan said, there is.
The monk said, can the one who's not ill still see the master or not?*
You can see this guy's getting confused.
*Dongshan said, I can still see him.
The monk said, well, what does the master see?
Dongshan said, when I observe him, I don't see any illness.*
*Dongshan said to the monks, when you leave the skin bag, you inhabit.
Where will you go and see me again?
The monks didn't answer.
So Dongshan recited a verse.
Students as numerous as the sands in the Ganges, but none are awakened.
They err by searching for the path in another person's mouth.
If you wish to forget form and not leave any traces, wholeheartedly strive to walk in emptiness.
Then Dongshan had his attendants help him shave his head, bathe, and get dressed.*
So implying that he's very weak and can't do these things on his own.
*And then he had a bell rung to summon the monks so he could bid them goodbye.
He appeared to have passed away.*
So he's lying there, you know.
*And the monks began wailing, piteously, without let up.
And suddenly Dongshan opened his eyes and said to them, homeless monks, please don't be attached to things.
That is authentic practice.
Why lament an arduous life and a pitiful death?
And so Dongshan then instructed the temple director to organize a delusion banquet.
The monk's adoration for Dongshan was unending.
So seven days later the food was prepared,*
so, big feast, it took seven days to get the delusion banquet ready.
*And Dongshan had a final meal with the congregation.
Then he said, don't make a big deal about it.
When I pass away, don't go carrying on about it.
Dongshan then returned to his room and sitting upright passed away.
It was the third month in the year 869.
Sixty-three years of age, he'd been an ordained monk for forty-two years.
Dongshan received the posthumous name Enlightened Source.
And his stupa was named Wisdom Awakening.*
He doesn't know what really happened, but it's a lovely story, I thought.
You'd like to hear that story of Dongshan trying to help his students as he was dying.
And that is our commitment, as practitioners of the Bodhisattva way: to help, whether we feel like it or not.
And what time would you most not feel like doing something?
In your dying moment, you might be a little tired.
You might not really feel like facing the facts of that moment.
You might have a preference that your monks would not be, how do you say, crying piteously without peace.
And yet, he understood.
Every moment unfolds the way it does, and we just turn towards it and help as best we can.
And if you can't be with the one you love, love the one you're with.
So maybe in these next weeks, if you want to, we could all take up the study of preferences.
Not trying to escape or suppress or somehow tinker with our life to reduce the preferences, but to turn towards them, to recognize them, to label them: oh, I have a preference.
I wish this was different than how it is.
And then, just to continue, just to continue living, to allow just awareness to be the response.

And have faith in mind, the title of that poem I read you half of, faith in the mind's ability to straighten itself out, little by little, as awareness is applied, so that preferences can arise and cease, just like every other phenomena in life.
We don't have to get so stuck, but if we are stuck, we just turn towards that and notice that.
Anyway, might be interesting.
Thank you for listening so patiently to my talk.
*May our intention equally penetrate every being and place with the truth.*
